name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippians will soon be able to participate in a school-choice tax credit program. Here’s what to know
description: Proponents of school choice policies say a new federal tax credit program is a win for the state. Opponents say it undermines Mississippi voters' rejection of school choice.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Starting next year, Mississippi families can get a break on their taxes for donating to scholarships that will largely benefit private schools, experts say. 
The federal program, created by President Donald Trump’s 2025 “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” will give people a break on their taxes for contributing to scholarships that can pay for education expenses at private schools, charter schools or public schools. Experts expect most of the money will flow toward private schools and families who could already afford, or were on the cusp of being able to afford, a private school education. 
Proponents of school-choice policies — which are aimed at giving families more educational options, often funding those choices with public money — say it’s a win for the state. 
But school-choice opponents argue the policies siphon money away from the public education system, which must serve every child, and force Mississippi into a program its residents have already said they don’t want. 
Republican state lawmakers, led by House Speaker Jason White, made a full-court push to expand school-choice policies in Mississippi earlier this year. However, House Bill 2, his lengthy school-choice bill, passed by a thin margin in the House and was killed by the Senate. 
Before that, in January, Gov. Tate Reeves announced that Mississippi would be participating in the federal tax credit scholarship program starting in 2027. States must opt in to that program. 
House Speaker Jason White, R-West, addresses state representatives as the House prepares to debate House Bill 2 on Thursday, Jan. 15, 2026, at the Capitol in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Douglas Carswell described it as an “awesome” program that allows the state to correct the Senate’s failure to expand school-choice options. He heads up the Mississippi Center for Public Policy, a conservative think tank that backs the expansion of school-choice policies.
Nancy Loome, a public school advocate and founder of The Parents’ Campaign, disagrees with Reeves’ decision. 
“Voters made it clear when House Bill 2 was debated in the 2026 legislative session that they don’t want this,” she said.
How does the federal tax credit program work?
The federal program allows taxpayers to contribute up to $1,700 each, or $3,400 for a married couple filing jointly, to an organization that awards school scholarships.
The governor designates scholarship-granting organizations, or SGOs, to award money to a school to cover costs of a child’s education. Taxpayers can’t direct their money to a particular student or school, but SGOs can focus on a particular group of students, like students who attend religious private schools. 
Reeves has not yet finalized his list of SGOs for Mississippi, according to the Mississippi Center for Public Policy, which is tracking and publishing the state’s eligible SGOs. The governor’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment. 
Donors will get a dollar-for-dollar tax credit, a break on their taxes equal to the amount they contribute, which is about three times as much as people receive from donating to a children’s hospital or other causes. 
Families who earn up to 300% of the area’s median income qualify to participate in the scholarship program. That’s six figures in Mississippi, or about $150,000. 
The House of Representatives debate House Bill 2 on Thursday, Jan. 15, 2026, at the State Capitol in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Paige Shoemaker DeMio, a senior policy analyst at Center for American Progress, a progressive policy and research institute, said the people who will benefit those most from the tax credit program are wealthy and owe $1,700 or more in taxes. Research about existing state tax credit scholarship programs back that up. 
“Statistically, people who are higher income owe that much in taxes,” she said.
There’s no set amount for the scholarships. The scholarship-granting organization sets the amount. 
And across the country, school-choice scholarships and vouchers provide anywhere between $4,000 to $9,000. Nationally, private school tuition averages about $13,000. That means while federal scholarships may make it easier for families on the cusp of being able to afford private schools, that education still may be unaffordable to the neediest families.
Will federal tax credit scholarships help students from low-income families?
There’s no requirement to prioritize the scholarships for low-income students. A majority of private school vouchers across the country go to students who could already afford and were attending private schools, according to research.
Carswell recognized the reality that the scholarships may miss low-income students. 
“We need to ensure that we have SGOs that provide access to private education for low-income families, too,” he said. “That’s why we need a broad range of SGOs that offer smaller schools, and not just established ones, access to the new source of funding.”
However, the governor has little power to tailor the program to the state’s students, Shoemaker DeMio said.
The federal regulations require Reeves to approve any SGOs that meet the minimum requirements. He can’t impose additional reporting or standards.
The lack of transparency and reporting requirements is a “huge lost opportunity,” said Mike Petrilli of the Fordham Institute, a national conservative-leaning education policy think tank.
“It’s very much a light touch,” he said. “We may never know if this is making a difference for kids.”
How will tax credit scholarships for private schools affect public ones?
There’s been some movement nationally to use the program to divert money to public schools, including public charter schools, Shoemaker DeMio said, but it’s tricky to understand how that would play out. Public schools do not charge students to attend. 
And the federal guidance regulating that part of the program hasn’t been made public yet, she said. It’s also unclear how much it will cost states to administer the program, which could include monitoring fraud, reviewing audits and other duties. 
The U.S. Department of Treasury estimates the tax-credit scholarship program, which begins all over the country in 2027, will cost taxpayers $26 billion in its first three years. That would make it the federal government’s largest education expense — more than Title I, which ensures that economically disadvantaged children receive a high-quality education, and the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, which guarantees children with disabilities receive an equitable education.
Members of the House of Representatives vote on House Bill 2, a school-choice proposal, on Thursday, Jan. 15, 2026, at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“We’d be spending as a country more on private schools than any other (public education) program,” Shoemaker DeMio said. That could mean spending less on public education in the future, which could be especially detrimental to a state like Mississippi that heavily relies on federal funding. 
But most concerning to DeMio is that Mississippi voters have already rejected school-choice programs through legislative action. 
“Any time school choice has been on a ballot, it has failed,” she said. “This is clearly not a popular program, but people have now found a way to get around the voters and ignore what Americans want. It’s incredibly frustrating.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: With property taxes on the ballot, New Hampshire’s caucus midterm turns hyperlocal
text:
Activists for the progressive group Kent Street Coalition meet near Concord Hospital on a frigid October morning to urge passersby to vote no on adopting a tax cap for their school district, a question on every New Hampshire ballot Nov. 3. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt, New Hampshire Bulletin)Pam Hicks has lived in Hollis her whole life. Not all of her neighbors have been so lucky.
The town’s rural charm, its scattered farms and orchards, and its highly ranked schools come with a price: eye-watering property taxes. Over the years, some families who moved there with kids figured that out, she says.
“We call it ‘educate and evacuate,’” she said. “They come in, the kids go through the school system, and then when their kids are graduating — their houses are for sale.” 
Hicks blames complacency on the Hollis Brookline Cooperative School Board and rising budgets. This year, she has a solution. When she votes Nov. 3, Hicks and every other Granite Stater will be asked whether they want to impose a cap on school district property taxes for the next two years. She plans to vote yes. 
“There’s no oversight for what they’re doing,” she said of the board. “So…let’s put some guardrails on.”
Not everyone is happy with that approach. 
New Hampshire’s tax cap ballot question has kicked off fierce debates and avid campaigns across the state, vaulting an issue normally reserved for spring meetings — school district budgets — into an already electric midterm election season. 
Suddenly property taxes, perhaps New Hampshire’s most animating and polarizing topic, have a dedicated space on a ballot otherwise reserved for partisan choices. In a year in which opinions on President Donald Trump’s second term have often stolen political oxygen, New Hampshire’s tax cap debate has managed to spawn mailers, signs, online advertisements, door-to-door campaigns, street corner demonstrations, and heated local meetings. 
To Democrats, who opposed adding the question to the ballot, the solution it offers is simplistic and potentially harmful to school districts. They say it subverts local control by bypassing the previous method to adopt a tax cap: at a town meeting, in the context of a budget. 
But Republicans say removing the debate from March town meetings is the point: Many residents are unhappy with rising school district budgets but too few of them attend the spring meetings to make a difference, they argue. Putting the measure on the November ballot will ensure a more representative sample of a district’s residents are heard, they say. 
The politics 
A successful “yes” vote on the ballot question would limit a school district in two ways. For two years, it would cap the total amount in local property taxes the school district could raise to the amount collected the previous year, adjusted for inflation and any new taxable property. It would also require the district to keep its School Administrative Unit spending to 6% of its overall budget for those two years. 
The measure requires the support of 60% of all voters who fill in the ballot question to pass. And whether or not the 2026 vote is successful, the law requires the question to appear on the ballot one more time, for another two-year approval period, in the 2028 presidential election. 
Once adopted, a school district’s tax cap can be overridden for a specific annual budget if at least 60% of voters at the school’s annual meeting in spring vote to do so. 
Polling suggests there is general support for the tax caps. A St. Anselm College poll conducted Oct. 19 to 20 found that 57% of likely New Hampshire voters supported the tax cap, including 83% of Republicans, 56% of undeclared voters, and 31% of Democrats. 
Yet as road signs and billboards blanket the state, it has been sometimes hard to separate the tax cap from broader politics. 
Some Republicans are hoping that not only does the ballot question lead to new school district tax caps, but that voters reward the Republican state candidates who put it on the ballot. In a midterm election environment traditionally difficult for the party in the White House, hyperlocal concerns with property tax could overpower unease with Trump, some believe. 
And some Democrats have argued Republican lawmakers passed the law specifically to drive that turnout. 
The messaging
Statewide organizations have helped drive messaging on both sides.
The Committee to Elect House Republicans helped launch a website, “NHPropertyTaxRelief.com,” advocating for voting “yes” on the tax cap, complete with a calculator claiming to show how much money a voter in a specific town with a specific home value could save.
The committee does not employ doorknockers. But after the September state primary, it did purchase nearly 10,000 yard signs urging “yes” on Question 2 and distributed them to the hundreds of Republican State House candidates it represents, said Chris Maidment, a Republican consultant who works with the committee. 
Asked Friday how many of those signs went out, Maidment ran a quick calculation. “There’s like 20 in my truck, so I guess like 9,980,” he joked. 
Because it has delegated advocacy to state legislative candidates, the committee’s “yes” campaign is necessarily entwined with Republican politics. Maidment says that’s by design.  
“The job of the Committee is to elect a Republican majority, and to win as many seats for Republicans as possible,” Maidment said. “And so, this tax cap question is more of a tool to help us do that rather than an effort to get this passed in all the various communities.”
On the other side, several organizations have mounted campaigns to oppose the ballot questions, including major teachers’ unions like the NEA-NH and AFT-NH and groups such as Engage NH and MomsRising NH.
On a frigid Wednesday morning near the Concord Hospital in late October, members of the progressive advocacy group Kent Street Coalition gathered to wave signs at passing cars urging a no vote.
Louise Spencer, a co-founder of the group, argued tax caps obfuscated the true cause of high property taxes: low state spending on education. While New Hampshire public schools collectively spend more per student than most states, the state ranks 50th in state per-pupil education aid. 
“If various spending needs to happen, and there’s this funding cap, then it’s not solving any of the problems. The real problem here is that the state is refusing to pay its fair share for public education,” Spencer said. 
The group, which organizes advocates but does not raise or spend campaign money, held other sign-waving events across the Concord area throughout the month. 
Residents on both sides of New Hampshire’s school district tax cap debate attend a meeting at the Hollis Brookline High School to voice their opinions, ahead of a Nov. 3 question on the general election ballot, Oct. 21, 2026. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt, New Hampshire Bulletin)
The local conversations
Despite the statewide campaigns, many of the liveliest conversations in recent weeks have taken place locally. In October, school boards across the state hosted information sessions, attempting to toe the line between informing constituents about the effects of a tax cap and advocating against it. And attendees of the meetings have brought plenty of opinions of their own. 
At an auditorium in the Hollis Brookline High School one Wednesday evening, the atmosphere was raw, bordering on explosive. 
Darlene Mann, the budget committee chairwoman for the Hollis Brookline Cooperative School Board, walked through a detail-laden presentation on the district’s current budget, tax rates, and the effect of the proposed tax cap to about 100 residents spread among the theater’s seats. 
The school board is already on track to propose a budget with taxation that would come under the proposed tax cap, Mann said. Additionally, the district already consistently keeps its administrative budget below 6% of the overall budget, she said. 
Still, Mann said the tax cap could force tough decisions in the event of unexpected costs from one year to the next, such as for diesel, health care, or food, all of which have risen recently. 
As they took to the microphone, some Hollis residents echoed that point.
“If we go over this tax cut, if this passes, and we go over the tax cut in our budget, what would we have to reduce?” Krista Whalan asked. 
Mann’s response: The district would have to reduce discretionary spending categories, including academic programs, technology, staff, extracurricular activities, sports, and operations, but it could not reduce its mandatory spending such as transportation, health insurance, special education services, and collective bargaining agreements. 
“I do trust the school boards, and I certainly trust our budget committees,” Whalan added. “They work extremely hard. This is not a simple process.”
But others asked why the tax cap would be so destructive if the district is already projected to obey it.
“I don’t understand why all the pushback from the school boards,” said Dave Perry. “And the point I’m coming from here is that there have been very large increases in the past, so the level of trust I have is low.”
Others took a more personal approach. Gerald Moore made his point with recent history. His tax bill in 2022 was $10,619, he said. It rose to $12,235 in 2023, to $13,069 in 2024, and to $13,981 in 2025. But the 2026 tax bill is set to be about $15,000, he said.
“I’m 82; I’m on fixed income,” he said, addressing the board. “And when you show me that everything is nice and even, and you’re doing a terrific job, and I see my taxes going up at the rate of 10% a year, when 70% plus of the budget goes to schools, I get the feeling that I’m down in Times Square watching a three-card monte game.”
One resident with kids in the school system, Mandy Hoffman, sympathized with the tax concerns. For every resident, finding the tax bill in their mailbox is an annual source of dread, she said. But she argued the tax cap would only delay the true costs of running the schools and lead to higher taxes down the line. 
“I fear that people are going to continue to open up their mailbox and not see any change and say, ‘Gosh, I voted a certain way. Why didn’t something happen?’” she said.
Like Hicks, Hoffman, who moved in six years ago, is enamored with Hollis. 
“We wanted our kids to be able to ride bikes just like we did,” she said in an interview. “We wanted our kids to be able to climb trees just like we did.” 
Hollis fit that bill. But a reduction of school services for her children is the one thing that might threaten her desire to stay, Hoffman said. 
“I don’t want my neighbors spending more,” she said. “I want my neighbors having a very smart budget with a great community and a great school system.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia governor pledges overhaul of outdated K-12 school funding formula
text:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger speaks to press on April 27, 2026 at an event in Richmond touting policy accomplished during her first 100 days in office. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)Gov. Abigail Spanberger said on Oct. 29 that she is committed to adjusting Virginia’s K-12 funding formula, after a state research group found it needs substantial changes and advanced a plan to hire an expert tasked with studying a new funding mechanism for up to 24 months. 
The existing formula is over 50 years old, does not adequately reflect the real costs of operating schools, and has forced local governments to spend far more on K-12 education than the state.
Virginia lawmakers approve plan to advance new K-12 school funding formula

While the governor did not set a firm timeline for preparing it for the next biennium’s budget in December 2027, Spanberger said in an interview with the Mercury last Thursday that she aims to complete this monumental task before the end of the current administration, which ends in 2029.
“I’d do it tomorrow if we could do it,” said Spanberger. “(However) that is not realistic, but we have to get it done before the end of our administration.”
She also argued that a modernized funding formula could help Virginia’s schools better address monetary gaps and meet student needs.
 Earlier efforts

States outside of Virginia have taken two to three years to reform their K-12 funding formulas, emphasizing the challenge such an undertaking poses for state governments.
In Virginia, lawmakers and the legislative branch have had to find alternative ways to get the necessary funds to Virginia’s schools.
One successful initiative to provide financial relief to localities for students with specific needs, such as those qualifying for free lunch, English as a second language, or special education, came during former Gov. L. Douglas Wilder’s administration 30 years ago.
In 1992, Virginia created its K–12 At-Risk Add-On funding provision and dedicated $46.9 million in the 1992-1994 biennium. 
The Governor’s Commission on Educational Opportunity for All Virginians found that educating students from low-income households costs more than the state’s basic school funding formula provides. The add-on was intended to provide additional state funding to help cover those costs.
Ultimately, the provision eventually became state law and has undergone multiple changes.
 Looking ahead

Spanberger’s administration, lawmakers and education leaders, including the Virginia Association of School Superintendents (VASS), are eager to reform the new funding formula.
Sarah Calveric, VASS president, said the association is emphasizing that it be a student-driven formula that would better address regional demographic differences and geographic needs. 
This method would also give school districts the ability to attract and retain staff through alignment with prevailing wages, and enable them to procure specialized resources such as mental health providers and literacy specialists.
“When you create a funding formula that is more student-driven, it helps keep the focus on the main thing, which is students, their specific needs, and the geographic trends that school divisions are addressing on a daily basis,” Calveric said to the Mercury.
Lawmakers will return to Richmond to discuss education legislation and other subjects starting on Jan. 13. 
During the 45-day session, which the governor could extend, the Virginia Department of Education is expected to select a consultant, who will begin work during session after publishing its formal service request and selecting a bid.
The consultant will have to include policy factors such as base funding per student, class sizes, extra weights for student needs, operating costs, transition provisions and the Local Composite Index, which determines what each locality can pay for its schools.
The process will also include input from education leaders and other key partners on shaping the new formula.
Spanberger said one challenge of such a large-scale change is the limited timeframe of a single-term governorship to complete the work in four years. 
With only three years and two months remaining, the administration is trying to be aggressive to keep the project moving forward.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Notwithstanding Mayor Wu’s claims, the ‘State of the Schools’ in Boston is not good
text:
THE REALITY OF public education in Boston is far from what Mayor Michelle Wu depicted in her recent State of the Schools address. Hiding behind the improvements she touted is a broken system with abysmal performance outcomes across every grade in the district. 
In the Boston Public Schools, seven out of every 10 third-graders can’t read or do math at grade level, which is also true for eighth-graders. The outcomes are far worse for Black and Latino students, multilingual learners, students with disabilities, and low-income students in Grades 3-8, with proficiency levels as low as 4 percent for some subgroups. 
It serves no benefit to students and families to push this truth aside or to dismiss this data point as “one number.” Our city must do better, and the first step to real improvement is acknowledging this grim reality, something Mayor Wu continues to fail to do.  
When asked head-on about these low performance outcomes, the mayor stumbled, citing “accountability metrics in the speech.” But the metrics she shared hardly show any accountability at all and fail to address the real issue: that the vast majority of the 44,000 students in BPS can’t read or do math at grade level.  
In the wake of the recent Next Chapter Boston education advocacy campaign, Mayor Wu called the group’s billboards “cynical” and “disgusting.” The billboards show a picture of a child’s eyes with the phrase “BPS IS FAILING HER,” while citing the factual data that shows why.  After the ads were pulled from the MBTA, despite prior approval, it’s clear our city’s leaders are too fearful to come to terms with the truth.  
If anything, Mayor Wu’s education speech should be described as cynical, pointing to misleading numbers and increased investment in a handful of student clubs, instead of the systemic academic overhauls that are required for improvement. In one year, the mayor announced, BPS went from six math clubs to 22 (out of 104 schools) at a time when only 33 percent of 10th-graders are doing math on grade level. For English learners, this number drops to 10 percent, and for students with disabilities it is 6 percent. 
Mayor Wu mentioned that BPS had their highest graduation rate last year, but seniors at BPS need only a D- to prove “competency” and pass core courses. Meanwhile, without MCAS as a graduation requirement, is a BPS diploma worth what it claims with standards set so low? 
The mayor also noted that Boston’s third-grade reading scores have ranked at the top of its urban school district cohort for each of the past six years. But this is disingenuous framing that makes it appear as if reading scores are actually good.  
In reality, just 29 percent of BPS students in grades 3-8 met state proficiency in reading and math on the 2026 MCAS, compared with the statewide average of 40 percent — itself a worrisome statistic.  
Our state leaders, who consistently cheerlead about Massachusetts’s number one national ranking, also need to come clean about the crisis in education that we’re experiencing. The ranking that really needs their focus is that the Commonwealth also holds the distinction of having some of the largest achievement gaps in the country. 
BPS uses its own Focus early literacy curriculum, which has been in place for more than 10 years with little results. Teachers and school administrators have voiced concerns about this curriculum and have seen no change from the district.  
The mayor spent a significant amount of time in her speech celebrating the expansion of free weekend sports, opening vocational programs at Madison Park to the community,  and expanding early college. These “nice-to-have” additions are not what BPS should be focusing on given its true state of crisis. We need real academic overhauls, acceleration academies on school breaks, and ongoing data sharing and dissemination practices to set real benchmarks for improvements across every grade.   
To continue to pretend like our schools are better than they really are is a disservice to students, teachers, families, and the city at large. The same is true of painting a picture of widespread progress when not nearly enough is being done to address our deep-rooted issues.  
The mayor also promised to set five-year targets that will improve poor performances, like attendance rates and test scores. These goals are meaningless if they don’t include concrete, measurable benchmarks. The updated 2026-2031 Strategic Roadmap for BPS, introduced at the beginning of this academic year, reads more like a roadblock. It’s vague and neglects to establish real plans or standards for needed growth.  
With years to create this plan, why are district leaders overlooking such essential details? We need to set real, achievable targets for improvements across all grades in reading, writing, math, and science, and develop a step-by-step implementation strategy to do this. 
These can’t be goals that keep getting pushed back to far-future dates. We have to create policies that make change for students now, so our city can live up to the true promise of delivering a quality public education to all students.  
With a total budget of $1.7 billion, per-pupil spending in Boston is among the highest in the nation, at roughly $37,000 per student. With such deep pockets, you would think it would be easier to integrate a concrete plan for improvement in literacy and numeracy among students. The question is not whether we invest enough money in our schools, but whether we are putting this money in the right places to achieve better results versus paying for the same mistakes year after year. 
The challenges BPS faces, whether they are academic or operational, are compounding. From literacy and math scores to chronic absenteeism to a $200 million transportation system that seems incapable of delivering students to school on time, all performance indicators are either stagnant or moving in the wrong direction.  The “fix” requires both immediate interventions and long-term policy shifts.  
This starts with true oversight and accountability standards that directly tie district funding to verifiable student benchmarks, operational efficiencies, and a guarantee that all students are safe within their school environments. Today, none of these three critical levers for change are evident.  
If the mayor is truly committed to making BPS the “best in the nation,” she and other city leaders must come to terms with the fact that we cannot achieve this without first recognizing where we are drastically falling short. And despite what Mayor Wu has stated publicly, this campaign is not aimed at families, students, or teachers; it is aimed at the people who have the power to change this. 
Mary Tamer, a former member of the Boston School Committee, is the executive director of MassPotential, a fiscally sponsored program of the Goodnation Foundation. Next Chapter Boston is an initiative of MassPotential. Vernée Wilkinson is the director of the Family Advisory Board at SchoolFacts Boston, a nonprofit working to improve education for all in Boston.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Canyon County judge declines to halt pro-Prop 1 ballot initiative ads amid lawsuit
text:
Volunteers pass boxes of signatures supporting a ballot initiative to end Idaho's strict ban on abortion on July 2, 2026, outside the state Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun)This story was first published by Boise State Public Radio on Oct. 30, 2026.
A Canyon County judge has rejected a request by anti-Proposition 1 campaigners to halt TV ads from airing that promote the ballot measure days before the election.
In an opinion released late Friday night, Judge Davis VanderVelde found the ads did not violate Idaho campaign finance laws and declined to keep them from being broadcast by local stations.
A Republican Party operative and three board members of Too Extreme for Idaho, which opposes restoring abortion rights under Prop 1, filed their lawsuit Tuesday morning.
They said the scheme used by Idahoans United for Women and Families (IUWF), the Idaho Democratic Party and its gubernatorial candidate, Terri Pickens, concealed the true origin of who paid for the ads.
IUWF, which qualified Prop 1 for the ballot, gave the Idaho Democratic Party more than $720,000 in recent weeks. The party then purchased advertising through Pickens’ campaign.
All political candidates receive significant discounts on ads in the 60 days leading up to an election compared to political groups.
“Ultimately, Plaintiffs’ assertion that the monies from IUWF were specifically contributed for support of Proposition 1 with the intent of concealing the original donor for such advertisements requires logical leaps that are not fully supported by the evidence,” VanderVelde wrote.
Each of these transactions is publicly available in the state’s campaign finance database, which the plaintiffs cited in the evidence presented to the judge.
VanderVelde said there’s also no evidence showing that IUWF still controlled the hundreds of thousands of dollars it donated to the state Democratic Party.
An attorney for the defendants argued in court Thursday that the party had the final say in how any of that money was spent, which VanderVelde said was not proven otherwise by the plaintiffs.
“The Court recognizes that the parties have had a short time to advance this lawsuit and that if there was additional time, additional facts may be developed by either party which could lend further credence to their claims or defenses,” he wrote.
That said, the judge found there may still be outstanding legal questions about whether the ads are truly for a candidate or a proposition and whether the lower rates should apply.
“However, without further law or authority significant questions remain as to what constitutes an appropriate advertisement under the law in order to qualify as an advertisement promoting a candidate.”
Tom Luna, one of the plaintiffs, released a statement saying he and the three other men who brought the lawsuit disagree with the decision, but that it was important voters know who paid for the ads.
“I’m sure many voters are as mad as I am about these dirty tricks. Let’s make sure we turn our frustration into action by showing up on Election Day, making our voices heard, and standing for life,” Luna said.
A request for comment from the Idaho Democratic Party wasn’t immediately returned late Friday night.
